prime.problem: Seventeen systems cards can blur into seventeen unrelated tricks: a B-tree here, a cleaner there, a scheduler at the end. Without one lens you can't say why each design wins, or what it pays for the win.
prime.fits: The map of course 6. It builds on cs-5's partitioning and consistency and on cs-4's back-of-envelope sizing, and it frames every card here with one ratio: units touched per unit the question actually needs.
expect: C = U × A: useful work times amplification
idle capacity as amplification in a scheduler
prime.goal: For any card in the course, name what it amplifies, the design choice that sets that number, and what the design pays elsewhere.

attend: Which factor in C = U × A does a design control, and which one is fixed by the question being asked?
An LSM tree writes each byte about 20 times and a B-tree up to 41. Why does the overview still warn that those two numbers are not directly comparable?
What is the ‘unit’ of useful work for a scheduler, and what plays the role of amplification there?
When the 1 GB orders table fits 24 times into a laptop's RAM, which advice in this course stops applying?
Across the four families, which pairs of amplification trade against each other (reads vs writes, copying vs memory, idle vs fairness)?

must: The question fixes the useful work U → the design sets the amplification A → cost ≈ U × A → a better design lowers A, never U

Lowering one amplification usually raises another → B-tree cuts reads (250,000 → 1 page) but rewrites a 4 KB page per 100 B row → LSM cuts random writes (T·L = 20, sequential) but checks several runs per read → name all three before choosing
A copying design runs memory with a live fraction u → each byte freed costs u/(1−u) bytes copied → 9 at 90%, 19 at 95% → headroom (space) buys cheaper cleaning (copies)

Shared hardware held but not doing work is amplification too → FCFS, static quotas and half-placed gangs leave GPUs idle → fair share, DRF and backfill lower idle GPU-hours without breaking the head job's promise
elevated: Amplification counts units, not time → a sequential rewrite on disk is far cheaper than a random one, and a cached page read costs nanoseconds vs milliseconds → compare two A's only when they count the same kind of step on the same device
reference: the per-card headline numbers in the decision table (65,572 DB reads, M = 16,384, 70 → 15 derivations, 5.5 → 4.0 h)
the log-scale bar widths in the ‘what matters most’ chart
the reading list (DDIA chapters, RocksDB wiki, the FAST and VLDB papers)

compress.prompt: Close the overview and draw the whole course's causal map: one box per family (storage, memory and caching, batch and queries, scheduling), each with the thing it touches less of, the design choice that does it, and the arrow to what it pays. Then write three sentences on why A, not U, is the lever.
checklist: cost = useful work × amplification; the question fixes U, the design fixes A
storage: indexes and LSM trees trade read amplification against write amplification
memory: caches, anti-caching and log cleaning trade space (headroom, RAM) against misses and copies
batch and queries: combiners and semi-naïve evaluation avoid moving or re-deriving what is already known
scheduling: fair share, DRF and backfill turn idle GPU-hours into work, bounded by reservations and fairness
counts are not times: check the device and the kind of access before comparing

retrieve.q: Explain, using this course's orders table, why a full scan and a B-tree lookup differ by a factor of 250,000 even though they return the same row.
answer: U is one ~100 B row either way
the scan reads all 10⁷ ÷ 40 = 250,000 pages: A<sub>r</sub> = 250,000
the B-tree's top two levels are cached, so it reads 1 page from disk: A<sub>r</sub> = 1

retrieve.q: Walk through where the course's two write-amplification numbers come from: the LSM's 20 and the B-tree's 41.
answer: LSM: T = 10 per level × L = ⌈log₁₀(1 GB / 64 MB)⌉ = 2 levels = 20, written sequentially
B-tree: a 100 B row update rewrites its 4,096 B page ≈ 41, at a random location
41 is a worst case: batching several row updates per page write lowers it

retrieve.q: A team wants to run RAMCloud-style memory at 95% full to save RAM. Using the cleaning cost, argue what they give up and what a sensible target is.
answer: u/(1−u) at 0.95 = 19 bytes copied per byte freed, vs 9 at 90%
the cleaner then sets write throughput, not the clients
the paper's working range is 80–90%; the saved 5% of RAM doubles cleaning cost

retrieve.q: Which card would you reach for when a single 8-GPU job blocks a queue while GPUs sit idle, and which number on that card settles whether the fix helped?
answer: backfilling and gang scheduling: reserve the head job, fill holes
average wait 5.5 → 4.0 h and idle GPU-hours before t = 4: 16 → 10
check the head job still starts at its reservation (J1 at t = 4)

compare.q: cs-5's map is about where to coordinate; this one is about amplification. What does each treat as the scarce resource, and when does a cs-5 decision change a cs-6 number?
answer: cs-5: coordination (round trips, agreement, availability under partition)
cs-6: units touched per useful unit on one node or cluster
they meet when partitioning moves work: hash vs range keys decide whether a site's rows are one scan (Bigtable) or many
replication multiplies write amplification by the replica count

compare.q: cs-4 says everything is a trade-off. How does the amplification lens make that concrete enough to decide with numbers, and where does it still leave the choice to you?
answer: it names the three quantities that trade (read, write, space) and gives each a count
the counts are comparable only on the same device and access pattern
workload mix (read-heavy vs ingest-heavy) still decides which amplification matters most

predict.q: The course's table is 1 GB. Scale it to 1 TB with the same 64 MB memtable and T = 10. Commit first: what happens to the LSM's write amplification, and to the B-tree's height (fan-out 256)?
predict.answer: The LSM needs ⌈log₁₀ 16,384⌉ = 5 levels, so write amplification rises from 20 to about 50 (the LSM card computes this). The B-tree barely moves: 10¹⁰ rows at fan-out 256 is ⌈log₂₅₆ 10¹⁰⌉ = 5 levels instead of 3, and if the upper levels stay cached it is still about one disk read per lookup. Read amplification grows logarithmically in both; the LSM's write cost grows with every added level.

apply.task: Build an amplification ledger from memory. For each of these six swaps, write the wrong → right numbers and the design choice responsible: full scan → B-tree; no Bloom filter → Bloom filter (6 runs); no cache → LRU of 1,000; naïve → semi-naïve (6-node chain); bump-and-reprice → tape (500 parameters); FCFS → EASY backfill (8 GPUs). Then add one row of your own from another course, with its own counted U and A.
apply.done: All six rows match the overview's chart (250,000 → 1; 6 → 0.049; 200,000 → 65,572; 70 → 15; 501 → 1 + 1; 16 → 10 idle GPU-hours) and each has a one-line cause in your own words.
